title: Paula and Eustochium
hookLine: a Roman widow and her daughter who studied Hebrew and worked with Jerome

cards: A small boy on the shore stretches out his hands toward his mother, and his sister silently begs her to wait. The ship is ready to sail east.
Jerome tells this scene in the long letter he wrote about the mother after she died, and it's hard to read. She is Paula, a wealthy Roman widow. Beside her on deck is her daughter Eustochium.
Jerome says Paula lifted her eyes to heaven and didn't look back at the shore. He doesn't pretend it was easy; he says it tore at her. She was leaving a whole life behind for Bethlehem.

teach.h: A ROMAN WIDOW AND HER DAUGHTER.
teach.b: First, who they were. Paula came from the Roman nobility, and Eustochium was one of her daughters. Both had studied scripture in Rome in a circle of women Jerome taught, before any of them left.
In Bethlehem, Jerome says, Paula set out to learn Hebrew, so she could sing the psalms in the language they were written in. He says she managed it, and Eustochium too.
These weren't patrons who simply paid for a scholar's work. They were students of the text, reading it in the original alongside him. Third, the questions.
Jerome says Paula made him read through the scriptures with her.

teach.h: SHE WOULDN'T LET A QUESTION GO.
teach.b: When he hit a passage he couldn't explain, and honestly said so, she wouldn't let it go. She'd press him with fresh questions until he told her which meaning he thought most likely.
A student like that makes a teacher better. Fourth, what they built.

In Bethlehem, Paula founded communities for women living a life of prayer, and a place to welcome pilgrims. Jerome dedicated works to them, and after Paula died he wrote her long epitaph as a letter to Eustochium.
He says she died with verses of the psalms on her lips, the psalms she had worked so hard to learn. So Jerome's Bible didn't come from a scholar working alone.
In Bethlehem he worked alongside two women of the book who wouldn't stop asking.

how: Catholics honor Saint Paula and Saint Eustochium as saints, and Jerome's letters to and about them are among the main sources for their lives.

games.q: you're Paula, reading scripture with Jerome. he admits he can't explain a passage. what do you do?
games.why: Jerome says she wouldn't let it go: she kept asking until he told her which meaning he thought most likely.

practice: Bring to mind a woman who knows something deeply and wouldn't let you read it carelessly, someone who pressed you with a question you couldn't answer yet, or sat with you over a hard page.
Remember one moment with her and hold it, with thanks; if she's gone, or out of reach, you can simply say her name. If you pray, thank God for her.

wordCard.voice: Paula. The Roman widow who left everything for Bethlehem, learned Hebrew, and pressed Jerome with questions about the scriptures. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: women of the book. Good questions are a gift to any teacher. That's seven hundred forty-three days.
